title: Stative Verbs: States & Actions
subtitle: Understand why meaning changes the form, then put the distinction into practice.

sections.label: Lesson Notes
sections.title: A state or an action?
sections.intro: We revisited stative verbs, their categories and the way some verbs change meaning when they describe an action.

cards.title: Start with meaning
cards.text: A stative verb often describes a condition, feeling, possession, perception or thought rather than an action in progress.

cards.title: The same word may change jobs
cards.text: Compare ‘I think it is useful’ (opinion) with ‘I’m thinking about it’ (an active mental process).

cards.title: Read the whole sentence
cards.text: Ask who is doing what. ‘The sauce tastes good’ describes a quality; ‘The chef is tasting the sauce’ describes a deliberate action.

cards.title: States: usually present simple
cards.text: Many stative meanings normally use the present simple, even when true now: ‘I know the answer’, ‘She owns the book’, ‘This smells good’. Avoid ‘I am knowing the answer’.

cards.title: Groups of meanings
cards.text: Common examples include mental states (know, understand, believe), feelings and preferences (like, love, prefer), possession (own, belong, have) and senses (hear, smell, taste). These are tendencies, not a rule that every use of a word is always stative.

cards.title: Think: opinion or process
cards.text: ‘I think this plan is useful’ expresses an opinion. ‘I’m thinking about the plan’ means I am considering it now. Present continuous is be + verb-ing: I am thinking; she is thinking.

cards.title: Taste and smell
cards.text: A quality uses a state meaning: ‘The soup tastes salty’ and ‘The flowers smell lovely’. An intentional action can be continuous: ‘The chef is tasting the soup’ and ‘She is smelling the flowers’.

cards.title: Have and see
cards.text: For possession, say ‘I have a car’, not normally ‘I’m having a car’. In an experience, continuous can work: ‘We’re having lunch’. ‘I see what you mean’ expresses understanding; ‘I’m seeing a friend tomorrow’ can mean a planned meeting.

cards.title: Be and temporary behaviour
cards.text: ‘She is helpful’ describes a quality. ‘She is being helpful today’ can describe behaviour at a particular time. This does not mean every adjective or every stative verb works in the continuous.

cards.title: believe
cards.text: Think something is true. ‘I believe this is the right answer.’

cards.title: belong
cards.text: Be owned by or be connected to someone. ‘This book belongs to my friend.’

cards.title: prefer
cards.text: Like one thing more than another. ‘I prefer quiet cafés.’

cards.title: taste
cards.text: Describe flavour or actively test food. ‘The soup tastes good.’ ‘The chef is tasting it.’

cards.title: smell
cards.text: Describe an odour or deliberately use your sense of smell. ‘It smells fresh.’ ‘She is smelling the flowers.’

cards.title: think about
cards.text: Consider something. ‘I’m thinking about my next lesson.’

activities.prompt: Correct: I am knowing the answer.
Change the opinion into an active process: I think about the plan. Make it clear that the person is considering it now.
activities.example: I’m thinking about the plan now.

activities.prompt: Match the meaning: ‘The soup tastes good’ / ‘The chef is tasting the soup’ — quality / deliberate action.
activities.example: The soup tastes good = quality. The chef is tasting the soup = deliberate action.

activities.prompt: Complete: She ___ (think) about the question at the moment.
activities.example: She is thinking about the question at the moment.

activities.prompt: Say one sentence with think for an opinion and one with thinking for an action.
activities.example: I think this lesson is useful. I’m thinking about my next goal.

readings.title: A sauce for dinner
readings.text:
A chef is making a new sauce. It smells wonderful, and a colleague thinks it will be popular. The chef is tasting the sauce now because she wants to check the flavour. She believes it needs a little more salt.

Her colleague owns a small café and enjoys trying new recipes. Today, he is helping the chef prepare dinner. He says the sauce tastes rich and offers a suggestion. The chef is thinking about his idea before making a final change.

questions.q: Why is the chef tasting the sauce?
questions.hint: Find the reason in the first paragraph.

sections.label: Listening
sections.title: Hear the contrast
sections.intro: Listen to the original examples, then repeat them. You can also read the script below.
sections.audioText: I think the sauce tastes wonderful. The chef is tasting it now. She is thinking about adding a little more salt. The flowers smell lovely, and a guest is smelling them.

activities.prompt: Which two actions are happening now?
activities.example: The chef is tasting the sauce, and she is thinking about adding salt. A guest is also smelling the flowers.

questions.q: Choose the natural sentence for an opinion.
opt: I am think this plan is useful.
I think this plan is useful.
questions.hint: Think for an opinion usually uses present simple.

questions.q: Complete: She ___ about the answer now.

opt: The chef is tasting the sauce.
I am having a car for years.
questions.hint: Have for possession is normally stative.

questions.q: Which sentence describes a deliberate action?
opt: The chef is tasting the soup.
questions.hint: Someone is actively testing the food.

questions.q: Complete: This book ___ to my friend.
questions.hint: Belong is normally used as a state.

questions.q: Which pair contrasts an opinion with an active process?
opt: I have a book / I own a book
It smells good / It tastes good
I think it is useful / I’m thinking about it
I know it / I understand it
questions.hint: Look at the two meanings of think.

questions.q: What does ‘She is being helpful today’ describe?
Choose the natural sentence for understanding.
